programme.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Preparation
programme.qualificationName: Ducelio Security+ SY0-701 Exam Preparation Course (preparation only -- not a CompTIA-issued certification)

objectives.description: Differentiate the security control categories (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and control types (preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, directive), and select an appropriate control for a stated security requirement.

resources.title: CISA: Cybersecurity Best Practices

lessons.title: Core Security Principles and Zero Trust

objectives.description: Apply the CIA triad, non-repudiation and the AAA model (authentication, authorization, accounting) to a described scenario, and explain how a Zero Trust approach removes implicit trust from network location.

resources.title: CIA, AAA and Zero Trust in Practice
resources.body: Confidentiality, integrity and availability describe WHAT a security programme protects; authentication, authorization and accounting describe HOW an identity is proven, permitted and tracked. Non-repudiation means a party cannot credibly deny an action they took, typically achieved with a digital signature or an equivalent audit trail. Zero Trust takes these ideas further: instead of trusting a request because it originated inside a corporate network boundary, every request is authenticated, authorized and continuously re-validated on its own merits, regardless of where it comes from. A gap analysis compares an organisation's current posture against a target state to find where these principles are not yet fully applied. Deception techniques such as honeypots, honeynets, honeyfiles and honeytokens are deliberately planted decoys that reveal an attacker's presence without exposing real assets.

practicalActivities.title: Zero Trust Control-Plane Walkthrough
practicalActivities.instructions: A remote employee's laptop, already inside the corporate VPN, requests access to a finance database it has never accessed before. Using Zero Trust principles, list three checks that should still happen before access is granted, and explain why network location (being on the VPN) is not sufficient on its own.

objectives.description: Describe the stages of a governed change-management process (request, impact analysis, approval, implementation, rollback) and explain why unreviewed change is a security risk.

resources.title: Why Change Management Is a Security Control
resources.body: A governed change typically moves through five stages: a request for change describes what is proposed and why; an impact analysis identifies what systems, data or users could be affected; a change-advisory review approves, rejects or defers the request; implementation applies the change during an agreed window; and a rollback plan describes exactly how to reverse the change if something goes wrong. Skipping any of these stages is a common root cause of security incidents: an unreviewed firewall-rule change, for example, can silently open a path an attacker later uses, and without a rollback plan a failed change can turn a small mistake into an extended outage.

objectives.description: Compare symmetric and asymmetric encryption, explain the role of hashing and digital signatures, and identify when each cryptographic approach is appropriate for a described requirement.

resources.title: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary

practicalActivities.title: Certificate and TLS Handshake Inspection Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: Using a browser's built-in certificate viewer against a public HTTPS site of your choice, record the certificate's subject, issuer, validity dates and the negotiated TLS protocol version and cipher suite. Explain, in your own words, which cryptographic primitive (symmetric, asymmetric or hashing) is responsible for each of: encrypting the bulk data, establishing the shared session key, and proving the certificate has not been tampered with. Do not attempt to intercept, decrypt or tamper with traffic you do not own; this lab is observational only.

objectives.description: Classify common threat actor types (nation-state, organised crime, hacktivist, insider, unskilled attacker, shadow IT) by typical motivation, sophistication and resource level.

resources.title: Who Attacks, and Why
resources.body: Threat actors differ enormously in capability and motive. A nation-state actor typically has significant resources and patience, and is motivated by espionage or strategic advantage. Organised crime is financially motivated and increasingly professionalised. A hacktivist acts on ideological or political grounds, often favouring disruption or embarrassment over financial gain. An insider already has legitimate access, which makes their actions harder to detect regardless of skill level. An unskilled attacker relies on freely available tools rather than original technique. Shadow IT is not malicious by intent but still introduces risk: it describes technology adopted outside an organisation's approved and monitored processes.

practicalActivities.title: Threat Actor Profiling Exercise
practicalActivities.instructions: For each of three described incidents (a leaked customer database offered for sale on a forum, a defaced public website with a political message, and a former employee deleting shared files after resignation), identify the most likely threat-actor type and justify your answer using motivation and access level.

objectives.description: Identify common attack vectors (phishing and other social-engineering channels, removable media, wireless, direct network access, supply chain) and explain how each expands an organisation's attack surface.

resources.title: Vectors In, Surface Exposed
resources.body: An attack vector is the specific path an attacker uses to reach a target; the attack surface is the total set of points where an attacker could attempt entry. Phishing and other social-engineering channels are common attack vectors because they target people rather than systems. Removable media can carry malware past network-perimeter defences entirely. Wireless networks extend the attack surface beyond a building's physical walls. Direct network access matters most when perimeter controls are weak or absent. A supply-chain vector compromises a trusted third party (a software vendor or managed service provider) to reach the real target indirectly -- which is why vendor trust itself is a security control, not just a business relationship.

objectives.description: Distinguish categories of vulnerability (application, operating-system, hardware, cloud misconfiguration, zero-day, supply-chain) and describe why each requires a different mitigation approach.

resources.title: OWASP Top Ten Web Application Security Risks

objectives.description: Given a described scenario, recognise indicators of malware infection and common attack patterns (account lockouts, unusual resource consumption, anomalous logins, unexpected outbound traffic) and identify the likely malware family or attack type involved.

resources.title: Spotting the Signs
resources.body: Most compromises leave observable traces before, during and after the attacker's main objective. Repeated account lockouts can indicate a password-spraying or brute-force attempt. Unusual CPU, memory or network load on a normally quiet host can indicate cryptomining malware or a command-and-control beacon. A login from an impossible travel distance in a short time window suggests a stolen credential being used from a second location. Unexpected outbound traffic to an unfamiliar destination, especially shortly after a user opened an email attachment or link, is a classic indicator of a dropper or trojan establishing contact with an attacker-controlled server. None of these signs alone is proof of compromise, but together they build a case worth investigating.

practicalActivities.title: Indicator Triage Exercise
practicalActivities.instructions: You are given four short log excerpts: (1) one account with 40 failed logins in five minutes, (2) a workstation suddenly using 95% CPU overnight with no scheduled job running, (3) a login from a country the employee has never travelled to, occurring two minutes after their normal login from their home city, and (4) a spike in DNS queries to a newly registered domain. For each, name the most likely underlying cause and the first triage step you would take.

objectives.description: Explain how segmentation, hardening, least privilege, patch management, monitoring and access control work together to reduce risk from the threats and vulnerabilities studied earlier in this module.

resources.title: Defence Is a Combination, Not a Single Control
resources.body: No single mitigation stops every threat covered so far in this module; enterprises layer several together. Segmentation limits how far an attacker can move after an initial foothold. Hardening removes unnecessary services and default settings an attacker could otherwise exploit. Least privilege limits what a compromised account or process can actually do, shrinking the blast radius of any single breach. Patch management closes known vulnerabilities before they can be exploited at scale. Continuous monitoring turns the indicators from the previous lesson into an actionable alert. Access control ties identity to authorization so that even a valid credential cannot reach resources it was never granted. Together, these controls assume that some individual defence will eventually fail, and are designed so that failure does not automatically mean compromise.

objectives.description: Compare the security implications of common deployment models (on-premises, cloud, hybrid, infrastructure-as-code, serverless, microservices) in terms of availability, resilience, patch responsibility and shared responsibility.

resources.title: Choosing Where Workloads Live
resources.body: On-premises infrastructure gives an organisation full control, and full responsibility, over every layer. Cloud deployment shifts some of that responsibility to the provider under a shared-responsibility model: broadly, the provider secures the underlying infrastructure while the customer secures what they configure and put on it, though the exact split depends on the service model. Hybrid deployments combine both, and must be evaluated as a single connected system rather than two separate ones. Infrastructure-as-code, serverless computing and microservices change WHERE security work happens (in a code review and pipeline rather than a server console) without eliminating the need for it -- a misconfigured infrastructure-as-code template can still deploy an insecure resource, just faster and more consistently than a human could.

practicalActivities.title: Cloud Shared-Responsibility Mapping Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: A company runs a customer-facing web application on a public cloud provider's infrastructure-as-a-service offering, using the provider's managed database service and its own custom application code. For each of the following, state whether the CUSTOMER, the PROVIDER, or BOTH are responsible: physical data-centre security, the guest operating-system patches on a virtual machine the customer manages, the managed database's underlying software patching, the application's own authentication logic, and network firewall rules the customer configures. Justify any 'both' answer.

objectives.description: Explain how network segmentation, device placement (firewalls, load balancers, sensors) and secure connectivity choices reduce an enterprise network's exposure to attack.

resources.title: Placing Devices Where They Matter
resources.body: Segmentation divides a network into zones so that a compromise in one zone does not automatically grant access to another. A screened subnet (sometimes called a perimeter network) hosts public-facing services separately from the internal network, so that if a public server is compromised, the attacker still faces a boundary before reaching internal systems. Device placement matters as much as device choice: a firewall placed only at the internet edge does nothing to stop lateral movement once an attacker is already inside. Secure connectivity choices, such as requiring an encrypted tunnel for remote administrative access, reduce the chance that credentials or commands are exposed in transit.

practicalActivities.title: Network Segmentation Design Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: A small organisation currently has one flat network containing its public website server, its employee workstations, its finance database and a guest Wi-Fi access point, all on the same subnet. Propose a segmented design: list the zones you would create, which of the four assets belongs in each zone, and one control you would place at each zone boundary. Explain the specific risk your design removes compared to the current flat network.

objectives.description: Apply data classification and select an appropriate protection technique (encryption at rest, encryption in transit, tokenisation, masking, data-loss prevention) for a described data-handling scenario.

resources.title: Matching Protection to Data State and Sensitivity
resources.body: Data classification (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) determines how much protection a given dataset warrants. Encryption at rest protects data stored on disk; encryption in transit protects data moving across a network; the two are independent controls and a system can have one without the other. Tokenisation replaces a sensitive value with a non-sensitive substitute that can be mapped back only through a separately protected lookup, which is common for payment-card data. Masking obscures part of a value for display purposes (such as showing only the last four digits of an account number) without necessarily protecting the underlying stored value. Data-loss prevention tooling inspects data leaving an organisation's control and blocks or flags transfers that violate a defined policy.

objectives.description: Explain how redundancy, backup strategy (including the 3-2-1 principle) and recovery-site choice (hot, warm, cold) support an organisation's availability and recovery objectives.

resources.title: Planning to Recover, Not Just to Prevent
resources.body: No preventive control is perfect, so resilience design assumes something will eventually fail and asks how quickly normal operation can resume. The 3-2-1 backup principle keeps three copies of data, on two different media types, with one copy stored off-site, so that no single disaster destroys every copy. A hot recovery site is fully staffed and running in near-real-time, offering the fastest recovery at the highest ongoing cost. A warm site has infrastructure in place but requires some setup before use. A cold site has space and power but little else pre-configured, offering the slowest recovery at the lowest cost. The right choice depends on how much downtime the organisation can actually tolerate.

practicalActivities.title: Backup and Recovery Strategy Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: An organisation's finance database must be recoverable within 4 hours (recovery time objective) with no more than 15 minutes of data loss (recovery point objective). Propose a backup schedule and recovery-site type that could meet these targets, and explain why a weekly full backup to a single on-site drive would fail to meet them.

objectives.description: Explain how a secure configuration baseline is established, deployed and maintained, and identify hardening techniques appropriate to different device types (endpoints, network devices, mobile, IoT).

resources.title: Baselines as a Living Standard
resources.body: A secure baseline is a documented, approved starting configuration for a device type, built by removing unnecessary services, changing default credentials and applying vendor-recommended settings. Establishing a baseline once is not enough: it must be deployed consistently across every matching device and then maintained, since new vulnerabilities and configuration drift both erode a baseline's protection over time. Hardening techniques differ by device type -- disabling unused services and enforcing endpoint protection on a workstation looks different from disabling unused management protocols on a network switch or restricting installed applications on a mobile device -- but the underlying goal is always the same: reduce the number of ways the device can be attacked.

practicalActivities.title: Endpoint Hardening Baseline Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: You are given a description of a newly imaged workstation: default administrator account still enabled, remote desktop open to the whole internal network, no host firewall configured, and three unused legacy protocols still running. Propose a hardening checklist of at least five specific changes, and for each explain which attack it is intended to prevent.

objectives.description: Describe the lifecycle of an IT asset from acquisition through classification, ownership assignment, inventory tracking and secure disposal, and explain the security risk of an unmanaged asset.

resources.title: You Cannot Secure What You Do Not Know You Own
resources.body: Asset management begins at acquisition and procurement, where a new device or software licence first enters an organisation's inventory. Each asset should be classified by sensitivity and assigned an owner accountable for its security. Ongoing inventory tracking, including enumeration sweeps that compare what should exist against what actually responds on the network, catches assets that were never formally logged -- these unmanaged assets are dangerous precisely because they receive no baseline, no patching and no monitoring. Secure disposal and decommissioning ensures that data is not recoverable from retired hardware and that the asset is formally removed from every system that still trusts it.

objectives.description: Explain the vulnerability-management cycle (scanning, prioritisation, remediation, validation) and prioritise a set of described vulnerabilities using severity and exploitability.

resources.title: From Scan Result to Closed Ticket
resources.body: Vulnerability management is a repeating cycle, not a one-time project. Scanning discovers vulnerabilities present in an environment. Prioritisation ranks them, typically weighing severity, exploitability, and whether the affected asset is reachable from an untrusted network, since a critical vulnerability on an isolated internal system may be a lower practical priority than a moderate one exposed to the internet. Remediation applies a fix -- a patch, a configuration change, or a compensating control when patching is not immediately possible. Validation confirms the fix actually closed the gap, because a remediation step that was applied but not verified is not meaningfully different from no remediation at all.

practicalActivities.title: Vulnerability Prioritisation Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: You receive a scan report listing four findings: (1) a critical remote-code-execution flaw on an internet-facing web server, (2) a critical flaw on a database server reachable only from one internal management subnet, (3) a moderate misconfiguration on an internal file server, and (4) a low-severity informational finding on a printer. Rank these four for remediation order and justify your ranking using both severity and exposure.

objectives.description: Explain how log aggregation, SIEM correlation, baseline deviation and network telemetry (NetFlow, packet capture) support detection of abnormal activity.

resources.title: Turning Raw Telemetry into a Useful Alert
resources.body: Individual log entries rarely tell a complete story on their own. Log aggregation collects entries from many systems into one place so they can be searched together. A security information and event management platform correlates those aggregated logs against defined rules, turning a pattern spread across several systems into a single actionable alert instead of dozens of isolated entries a human would have to connect manually. Baseline deviation detection flags activity that differs from an established normal pattern for a given user or system, which can catch novel attacks that do not match any known signature. Network telemetry such as NetFlow summarises WHO talked to WHOM and how much, while full packet capture records the actual traffic content for deeper investigation when a summary is not enough.

practicalActivities.title: SIEM Log Investigation Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: You are given a short set of correlated log excerpts showing: a successful VPN login from an unusual country, followed within two minutes by a login to an internal file server the same user has never accessed before, followed by a large outbound data transfer to an external address. Write a two-to-three sentence investigation summary describing what likely happened and the order of events, and list the first two containment actions you would take.

objectives.description: Explain how firewall rules, access control lists and network segmentation controls (screened subnets, intrusion detection/prevention) are configured and reviewed to enforce an enterprise security policy.

resources.title: Enforcing Policy at the Network Layer
resources.body: A firewall rule set translates security policy into an enforceable, ordered list of allow/deny decisions; rules should be as specific as possible and reviewed regularly, since an overly broad rule added temporarily for troubleshooting is a common source of lingering exposure. Access control lists are ordered permit/deny rules used to restrict access; on network devices they commonly filter traffic using attributes such as source, destination, protocol and port. Intrusion detection systems observe traffic and alert on suspicious patterns; intrusion prevention systems can additionally block matching traffic automatically. A screened subnet keeps public-facing systems separated from the internal network, so a rule allowing inbound web traffic never needs to reach further than that boundary.

practicalActivities.title: Firewall Rule Set Analysis Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: You are given a simplified five-rule firewall configuration for a small business, including one rule allowing 'any source, any destination, any port' inbound that a previous administrator added during troubleshooting and never removed. Identify which rule(s) violate least-privilege network access, explain the specific risk each poses, and propose a corrected, more specific replacement for the overly permissive rule.

objectives.description: Explain identity lifecycle operations (provisioning, deprovisioning, multifactor authentication, single sign-on, federation, privileged access management) and evaluate whether a described access configuration follows least privilege.

resources.title: Managing Identity Over Its Whole Lifecycle
resources.body: Provisioning grants a new identity the access it needs when it is created; deprovisioning removes that access promptly when it is no longer needed, and a delay here is one of the most common causes of orphaned accounts an attacker can later abuse. Multifactor authentication requires more than one proof of identity, so a stolen password alone is insufficient to authenticate. Single sign-on lets one authenticated session grant access across multiple applications, improving usability but concentrating risk on that one session. Federation extends trust across organisational boundaries, allowing an identity from one organisation to be recognised by another without a separate account. Privileged access management applies extra controls -- approval workflows, time-limited elevation, session recording -- specifically to the smaller set of accounts with elevated permissions.

practicalActivities.title: Access Control Configuration Review Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: You are given a described list of six employee accounts and their current permissions, including a marketing employee with database-administrator rights left over from a past project, and a former contractor's account that is still active. Identify every entry that violates least privilege, and for each, state the specific corrective action (revoke, downgrade, deprovision) you would take.

lessons.title: Automation and Orchestration in Security Operations

objectives.description: Explain how automation and orchestration (provisioning, guardrails, ticket creation/escalation, API integration) improve the speed and consistency of routine security operations tasks.

resources.title: Letting the System Do the Repeatable Work
resources.body: Automation performs a single well-defined task without human intervention, such as automatically provisioning a standard set of access when a new employee's record appears in the HR system. Orchestration coordinates multiple automated steps together into a larger workflow, such as automatically creating an investigation ticket, notifying the on-call analyst and applying a temporary network block the moment a high-confidence alert fires. Guardrails are the boundaries placed around automation so it cannot take an action beyond what was intended, which matters because automation executes exactly what it is told, consistently, including any mistake in how it was configured. Integrating these workflows through APIs lets otherwise-separate security tools act as one coordinated system rather than a set of manually bridged silos.

objectives.description: Describe the incident-response lifecycle (preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned) and explain the purpose of a tabletop exercise.

resources.title: The Incident Response Lifecycle
resources.body: Preparation happens before any incident: playbooks, contact lists and tooling are put in place in advance, because an incident is the wrong time to design a process for the first time. Detection identifies that something may be wrong; analysis confirms whether it is a genuine incident and scopes its extent. Containment limits further damage while the incident is still active, eradication removes the root cause, and recovery restores normal operation. Lessons learned closes the loop by reviewing what happened and updating playbooks and controls so a similar incident is handled better, or prevented outright, next time. A tabletop exercise rehearses this whole lifecycle as a structured discussion using a hypothetical scenario, without touching real systems, so gaps in the plan are found in a low-stakes setting rather than during a genuine incident.

practicalActivities.title: Incident Response Evidence Analysis Lab
practicalActivities.instructions: You are given a described incident timeline (initial phishing email, a compromised account, lateral movement to a file server, and a burst of file-encryption activity consistent with ransomware) along with a short list of available evidence items (email headers, authentication logs, file-server access logs, and a memory capture from the affected file server). For each lifecycle stage from detection through recovery, name the evidence item most useful to that stage and explain why.

lessons.title: Digital Forensics and Investigative Data Sources

objectives.description: Identify data sources (firewall, application, endpoint and OS logs, IDS/IPS alerts, vulnerability scans, packet captures) useful to a security investigation, and explain basic evidence-handling and chain-of-custody principles.

resources.title: Choosing the Right Evidence Source
resources.body: Different data sources answer different investigative questions. Firewall logs show what traffic crossed a network boundary and whether it was allowed or blocked. Application logs show what a specific piece of software did, often including which user performed which action. Endpoint and operating-system logs show activity on an individual device, including process execution and file access. IDS/IPS alerts flag traffic matching known attack signatures. Vulnerability scan history shows what weaknesses existed on a system before an incident, which helps explain how an attacker got in. Packet captures preserve raw network traffic for deep analysis when summarised logs are not detailed enough. Chain of custody documents who collected each piece of evidence, when, and how it was stored, so that its integrity can be demonstrated later; evidence handled without a clear chain of custody is far less useful, because its authenticity cannot be established.

objectives.description: Explain the role of policies, standards, procedures and governance structures (boards, committees, defined roles such as data owner and custodian) in an organisation's security programme.

resources.title: The Governance Hierarchy
resources.body: A policy states WHAT an organisation requires and why, at a level intended to remain stable over time. A standard makes a policy specific and measurable, such as a minimum password length. A procedure describes step by step HOW a standard is actually carried out. Governance structures such as a security steering committee provide oversight, approve significant policy changes and ensure accountability. Defined roles matter too: a data owner is accountable for a dataset's classification and protection requirements, while a data custodian implements the technical controls that protect it day to day -- distinguishing accountability from implementation keeps responsibility clear even as staff and systems change.

objectives.description: Apply the risk-management process (identification, qualitative and quantitative analysis including single loss expectancy, annualised loss expectancy and annualised rate of occurrence, a risk register, tolerance/appetite, and response strategies of accept, avoid, transfer and mitigate) to a described scenario.

resources.title: Turning Uncertainty into a Decision
resources.body: Risk management begins with identifying what could go wrong, then analysing it. Qualitative analysis ranks risks using descriptive scales such as low/medium/high. Quantitative analysis assigns numbers: single loss expectancy estimates the cost of one occurrence, annualised rate of occurrence estimates how often it is expected per year, and multiplying the two gives annualised loss expectancy -- an estimated yearly cost that can be compared directly against the cost of a proposed control. A risk register records identified risks, their analysis and their current treatment in one place. Risk tolerance and appetite describe how much risk an organisation is willing to accept before acting. Once a risk is understood, an organisation chooses to accept it (take no further action), avoid it (stop the risky activity), transfer it (such as through insurance), or mitigate it (reduce its likelihood or impact with a control).

practicalActivities.title: Quantitative Risk Calculation Exercise
practicalActivities.instructions: A described data-breach scenario has an estimated single loss expectancy of $50,000 and an estimated annualised rate of occurrence of 0.2 (expected once every five years). Calculate the annualised loss expectancy, and state whether a proposed control costing $8,000 per year to reduce the annualised rate of occurrence to 0.05 appears cost-justified, showing your reasoning.

objectives.description: Explain how vendor evaluation, service-level agreements and due-diligence review reduce risk introduced by third parties and supply-chain relationships.

resources.title: Your Risk Does Not End at Your Own Network
resources.body: A vendor with access to an organisation's data or systems extends that organisation's attack surface, even though the vendor is not directly under its control. Vendor evaluation assesses a prospective vendor's own security posture before a relationship begins. A service-level agreement sets measurable expectations, such as guaranteed uptime or a maximum notification time after a security incident, that can be enforced contractually. Due-diligence review, repeated periodically rather than only at onboarding, checks whether a vendor's actual practices still match what was promised, since a vendor's security posture can change significantly after the initial contract is signed.

objectives.description: Explain why organisations must track applicable regulatory and contractual compliance requirements and describe the consequences of non-compliance.

resources.title: Compliance as a Floor, Not a Ceiling
resources.body: Compliance requirements come from multiple sources at once: government regulation, industry standards an organisation has contractually agreed to follow, and requirements imposed by business partners. Tracking which requirements apply to a given system or dataset is itself a security-management task, since the same data may be subject to more than one framework simultaneously. Consequences of non-compliance can include financial penalties, loss of the ability to operate in a given market or industry, and reputational damage that outlasts the immediate incident. It is worth remembering that meeting compliance requirements is a necessary floor, not a guarantee of actual security -- a system can be compliant on paper and still be vulnerable in practice.

objectives.description: Distinguish internal from external audits, describe common attestation report types, and explain the purpose of a gap analysis following an assessment.

resources.title: Checking Your Own Work, and Having Others Check It
resources.body: An internal audit is performed by an organisation's own staff or an internal audit function, and is often used to prepare for a later external review. An external audit is performed by an independent third party and typically carries more weight with customers, regulators and business partners because of that independence. Attestation reports formalise an external auditor's findings; different report types (some naming a point-in-time review, others covering a period of operating effectiveness) answer different questions about whether a control merely exists or was actually operating consistently over time. A gap analysis performed after an audit or assessment compares current practice against the required or desired state and produces a prioritised list of what still needs to change -- the audit finds the gaps, but the organisation still has to decide what to do about them.

objectives.description: Design an outline security-awareness activity (such as a phishing simulation or onboarding briefing) appropriate for a described workforce, and explain how reporting mechanisms reinforce the programme.

resources.title: Turning Every Employee into a Sensor
resources.body: Technical controls alone cannot stop every attack, particularly ones that target human judgement directly, such as phishing. Security-awareness activities build the habits and recognition skills employees need to be a meaningful line of defence rather than the weakest link. An onboarding briefing sets expectations from day one; a periodic phishing simulation tests and reinforces recognition skills in a safe, controlled way; ongoing reminders keep the topic from fading from attention between formal sessions. A clear, low-friction reporting mechanism -- employees knowing exactly how and where to report something suspicious -- multiplies the value of awareness training, because even well-trained employees are only useful to the programme if reporting what they notice is easy enough that they actually do it.

assignmentTemplates.title: Security Control Mapping Assignment
assignmentTemplates.instructions: Select three safeguards used in a typical small-business office (for example a badge reader, an acceptable-use policy, and a locked server cabinet). For each safeguard, identify its security control category and its control type, then justify your classification in two to three original sentences.

rubric.description: Correctly identifies the control category for all three safeguards
Correctly identifies the control type for all three safeguards
Justification is clear, original and specific to each safeguard

assignmentTemplates.title: Incident Response Playbook Assignment
assignmentTemplates.instructions: Draft a one-page incident-response playbook outline for a described phishing-led account-compromise scenario, covering preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons-learned steps in your own words. Each stage should include at least one concrete action specific to the scenario, not a generic restatement of the stage name.

rubric.description: All seven lifecycle stages are present and correctly sequenced
Each stage includes a concrete, scenario-specific action
Playbook is written in the learner's own original words

assignmentTemplates.title: Vendor Risk Assessment Assignment
assignmentTemplates.instructions: Evaluate a described third-party payment-processing vendor against three risk criteria of your choice (for example data-handling practices, incident-notification commitments, and audit history). Recommend whether the organisation should proceed, proceed with conditions, or decline the vendor relationship, and justify the recommendation.

rubric.description: Selects three relevant, well-explained risk criteria
Evaluation of each criterion is specific to the described vendor
Final recommendation is clearly stated and justified

assessmentTemplates.title: Quiz 1: General Security Concepts Checkpoint
assessmentTemplates.instructions: Answer each question independently, in your own words.

questions.prompt: Which two properties, together with confidentiality, make up the CIA triad, and what does each protect against?
questions.expectedAnswer: Integrity protects against unauthorised or accidental modification of data; availability protects against data or systems being inaccessible when needed by an authorised user.
questions.markingGuidance: Award full marks for both properties correctly named with an accurate description of what each protects against; award half marks if only one property is correctly described.

questions.prompt: In the AAA model, what is the difference between authentication and authorization?
questions.expectedAnswer: Authentication confirms an identity claim (proving who someone is); authorization determines what an already-authenticated identity is permitted to do.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require both terms distinguished correctly and in the right order; partial marks if only one is correctly defined.

questions.prompt: What does non-repudiation mean in a security context, and name one mechanism that provides it.
questions.expectedAnswer: Non-repudiation means a party cannot credibly deny having performed an action; a digital signature is a mechanism that provides it.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require an accurate definition plus a valid supporting mechanism; partial marks for a correct definition alone.

questions.prompt: Explain why a Zero Trust approach does not automatically trust traffic just because it originates inside a corporate network.
questions.expectedAnswer: Zero Trust requires every access request to be authenticated, authorized and continuously validated regardless of network location, because an attacker who reaches the internal network should not automatically be trusted merely because of where the request originates.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the explanation to reference continuous verification independent of location, not merely restate the term.

assessmentTemplates.title: Quiz 2: Threats and Indicators Checkpoint
assessmentTemplates.instructions: Answer each question independently, in your own words.

questions.prompt: A workstation begins sending large volumes of outbound traffic to an unfamiliar external address shortly after a user opened an email attachment. What class of indicator does this describe, and what is one plausible cause?
questions.expectedAnswer: This is an anomalous/unexpected outbound network traffic indicator; a plausible cause is a dropper or trojan delivered by the attachment establishing contact with an attacker-controlled command-and-control server.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the indicator class named and a plausible malware-related cause given.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a worm and a trojan in terms of how each propagates?
questions.expectedAnswer: A worm self-propagates across a network without requiring user action, while a trojan disguises itself as legitimate software and relies on a user being tricked into running it.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require both propagation mechanisms described accurately.

questions.prompt: Describe one indicator that might suggest an account has been compromised through credential theft.
questions.expectedAnswer: A login from an impossible-travel location shortly after a legitimate login from a different location is one such indicator, since it suggests the same credential is being used from two places that cannot both be the genuine user.
questions.markingGuidance: Any valid, clearly explained indicator (impossible travel, unfamiliar device, unusual login time) earns full marks.

questions.prompt: Why is out-of-cycle or missing log activity itself considered a potential indicator of compromise?
questions.expectedAnswer: An attacker who gains sufficient access may disable or tamper with logging to hide their activity, so unexplained gaps or irregular logging patterns can themselves be evidence that something was deliberately hidden.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the answer to connect the missing logs to a deliberate attempt at concealment, not merely note that logs are missing.

assessmentTemplates.title: Midterm: Security Architecture Checkpoint
assessmentTemplates.instructions: Answer each question independently, in your own words.

questions.prompt: In a cloud shared-responsibility model, which party is typically responsible for the physical security of the data centre, and which is typically responsible for the customer's own application-level authentication logic?
questions.expectedAnswer: The cloud provider is typically responsible for physical data-centre security; the customer is typically responsible for their own application's authentication logic.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require both parts correctly assigned.

questions.prompt: Name two security advantages a hybrid deployment can offer over a purely on-premises deployment.
questions.expectedAnswer: Possible advantages include elastic capacity for disaster recovery/failover, access to a cloud provider's own security tooling and expertise, and the ability to keep the most sensitive workloads on-premises while offloading less sensitive workloads.
questions.markingGuidance: Award marks for any two distinct, well-reasoned advantages.

questions.prompt: Explain why a misconfigured infrastructure-as-code template can be a more serious risk than a single misconfigured server.
questions.expectedAnswer: An infrastructure-as-code template is typically reused to provision many resources, so a single flaw in the template can replicate the same misconfiguration across every resource it deploys, rather than affecting only one server.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the answer to reference the repeatable/scaled nature of the risk.

questions.prompt: Describe one potential security benefit of a well-designed microservices architecture compared with a monolithic application.
questions.expectedAnswer: A well-designed microservices architecture can isolate services from one another with least-privilege boundaries, so a vulnerability or compromise in one service does not automatically grant access to every other service, reducing the blast radius compared with a monolith where a single flaw can expose the whole application. This benefit depends on the isolation actually being designed and enforced; microservices are not automatically more secure than a monolith.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the isolation/blast-radius benefit to be clearly explained as conditional on deliberate design (least privilege between services), not stated as an automatic property of microservices.

questions.prompt: Give one patch-management challenge that is different for a serverless deployment compared to a traditional on-premises server.
questions.expectedAnswer: In a serverless deployment the underlying runtime/OS patching is generally the provider's responsibility, so the customer's patch-management focus shifts almost entirely to their own application code and dependencies rather than the operating system.
questions.markingGuidance: Award marks for any accurate, clearly explained contrast.

questions.prompt: Why must an on-premises deployment's owner accept full responsibility for both availability and patching, with no shared-responsibility split?
questions.expectedAnswer: Because the organisation owns and operates every layer of the stack itself -- physical hardware, operating system, and application -- there is no external provider to share any part of that responsibility with.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the answer to connect full ownership of every layer to full responsibility.

assessmentTemplates.title: Quiz 3: Vulnerability Management Checkpoint
assessmentTemplates.instructions: Answer each question independently, in your own words.

questions.prompt: List the four stages of the vulnerability-management cycle in order.
questions.expectedAnswer: Scanning, prioritisation, remediation, validation.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require all four stages named in the correct order.

questions.prompt: Why might a critical-severity vulnerability on an internal-only system be a lower practical priority than a moderate-severity vulnerability on an internet-facing system?
questions.expectedAnswer: Exploitability depends on reachability as well as severity; a vulnerability that is not exposed to an untrusted network is harder for a remote attacker to reach, so exposure must be weighed alongside raw severity when prioritising.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the answer to explain the role of exposure/reachability, not just restate severity.

questions.prompt: What is a compensating control, and when would a team use one instead of patching directly?
questions.expectedAnswer: A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the primary fix (such as a patch) cannot be applied immediately; a team might use one when a patch is not yet available or would break a critical system, to reduce risk in the meantime.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require both the definition and a valid reason for use.

questions.prompt: Why is the validation step necessary after remediation has been applied?
questions.expectedAnswer: Validation confirms the fix actually closed the vulnerability; without it, a remediation step that was applied but did not work as intended could be mistakenly treated as resolved.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the answer to explain that an unverified fix cannot be trusted to have worked.

assessmentTemplates.title: Quiz 4: Incident Response Checkpoint
assessmentTemplates.instructions: Answer each question independently, in your own words.

questions.prompt: List the incident-response lifecycle stages in order.
questions.expectedAnswer: Preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require all stages named in the correct order; partial marks for correct stages in the wrong order.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between containment and eradication?
questions.expectedAnswer: Containment limits further damage while an incident is still active, without necessarily removing the root cause; eradication removes the root cause itself, such as deleting malware or closing the exploited vulnerability.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require both stages correctly distinguished.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a tabletop exercise, and why is it performed without touching real systems?
questions.expectedAnswer: A tabletop exercise rehearses the incident-response lifecycle as a structured discussion using a hypothetical scenario; it does not touch real systems so that gaps in the plan can be found safely, without the risk or cost of disrupting live operations.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require both the purpose and the reason for avoiding real systems.

questions.prompt: Why does the lessons-learned stage matter even after an incident has already been fully recovered from?
questions.expectedAnswer: Lessons learned reviews what happened and updates playbooks and controls so that a similar incident is prevented or handled better in the future; without it, the same gap that allowed this incident could allow a repeat.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the answer to connect the review to future prevention/improvement, not just note that a review happens.

assessmentTemplates.title: Final Assessment: Risk Management Checkpoint
assessmentTemplates.instructions: Answer each question independently, in your own words.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative risk analysis?
questions.expectedAnswer: Qualitative analysis ranks risk using descriptive scales such as low/medium/high; quantitative analysis assigns numeric values such as single loss expectancy and annualised loss expectancy.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require both approaches correctly described.

questions.prompt: Given a single loss expectancy of $20,000 and an annualised rate of occurrence of 0.5, calculate the annualised loss expectancy and show your working.
questions.expectedAnswer: Annualised loss expectancy = single loss expectancy x annualised rate of occurrence = $20,000 x 0.5 = $10,000.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the correct formula applied and the correct numeric result shown.

questions.prompt: Name the four risk response strategies and give a one-sentence example of each.
questions.expectedAnswer: Accept (take no further action and absorb the risk), avoid (stop the risky activity entirely), transfer (such as purchasing insurance), mitigate (apply a control to reduce likelihood or impact).
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require all four strategies named with a valid example each.

questions.prompt: What is a risk register, and why is it kept as a single ongoing record rather than recreated for each assessment?
questions.expectedAnswer: A risk register records identified risks, their analysis and their current treatment in one place; keeping it as a single ongoing record lets an organisation track how risks and their treatments change over time rather than losing that history with each new assessment.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require both the definition and the reason for its ongoing nature.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between risk tolerance and risk appetite.
questions.expectedAnswer: Risk appetite describes the general amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to pursue or retain in principle; risk tolerance describes the acceptable variation around that appetite for a specific risk or objective.
questions.markingGuidance: Award full marks for a reasonable, clearly explained distinction between the general/strategic and specific/operational framing.

questions.prompt: Why can two organisations with the same risk appetite still make different decisions about the same described risk?
questions.expectedAnswer: Their specific tolerance thresholds, existing controls, financial capacity to absorb loss, and business context can differ, so the same general appetite for risk can still lead to different concrete decisions in a specific situation.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require a reasoned explanation, not merely restating that organisations differ.

questions.prompt: A proposed control costs $15,000 per year and would reduce annualised loss expectancy from $18,000 to $4,000. Is the control cost-justified? Show your reasoning.
questions.expectedAnswer: The control reduces annualised loss expectancy by $14,000 ($18,000 minus $4,000), which is less than the control's $15,000 annual cost, so on a purely financial basis the control is not cost-justified.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the correct reduction calculated and compared against the control cost, with a correct conclusion.

questions.prompt: Summarise, in your own words, why risk management is described as a continuous process rather than a one-time activity.
questions.expectedAnswer: New risks emerge and existing risks change in likelihood or impact as an organisation's technology, threat landscape and business context evolve, so a risk assessment performed once becomes outdated and must be revisited on an ongoing basis.
questions.markingGuidance: Full marks require the answer to explain that risk conditions change over time, not merely assert that risk management is continuous.
